REPORT
I. INTRODUCTION
 
The Department of Women and Child Development which became a full-fledged Ministry w.e.f. 30th January, 2006 is the nodal agency for all matters pertaining to the welfare, development and empowerment of women and children in the country. In this process various initiatives, policies, programmes, schemes and enabling measures have been evolved for the benefit of these groups covering a wide range of areas from gender equality, women and child related legislation to their social and economic rehabilitation. The schemes/programmes of the Ministry are implemented mainly with the support of State Governments, other
Government agencies and non-governmental organizations.
The Secretary informed the Committee that after elevation of the Department to a full-fledged Ministry, the following items have also been brought under its jurisdiction:-
 Additional Item Transferred from
(i) Early childhood Education Department of Elementary Education and Literacy
(ii) Juvenile Justice as a subject including all the establishments and laws under it. Department of Social Justice & Empowerment
(iii) Adoption including all the agencies and laws. Department of Social Justice & Empowerment
(iv) Child Welfare and Child Protection. Department of Social Justice & Empowerment
 
1.3       The Secretary also mentioned that funds allocated for the new schemes were not adequate when compared to programmes like ICDS covering only children of 0-6 age-group. The Secretary was of the view that for the welfare of children, all categories of children whether out of school or below poverty line, abused children, etc., a scheme of the size and level of ICDS was required. A comprehensive Bill for prevention of child abuse was also under preparation.
1.4       The Secretary then briefed the Committee about the achievements of the Ministry during 2005-06. Due to the good teamwork of the Ministry and co-ordinated timely action by the State Governments 467 additional projects and 1,88,000 Anganwadis Centres could be sanctioned under the ICDS scheme. State Governments were in the process of operationalising the Anganwadi Centres and getting the team of workers trained and placed in the field. A Cabinet Note for further expansion of approximately 1,10,000 Anganwadi Centres based on the new population norms has also been prepared. The Secretary also informed the
Committee that Cabinet approval has been obtained for doubling the number of creches under the Rajiv Gandhi Creche Scheme. Between January and March 2006, 7000 creches have been sanctioned and another 7719 creches will be added during 2006-07. Allocation per creche has also been enhanced from Rs.18,000 to Rs.42,000. Secretary also drew the attention of the Committee to the exemplary work done under Women Empowerment Programmes like STEP, Rashtriya Mahila Kosh and  Short Stay Homes.
1.5       The Committee appreciates the Government’s move to bring all the child related issues under one Ministry and desires that all out efforts should be made by the Ministry in implementing these schemes in an effective way.
II.        BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
2.1       The Committee notes that the plan allocation for the Ministry has been increased from  Rs. 3875.29 crore in 2005-2006 to Rs. 4795.85 crore in 2006-2007. The increase of Rs. 920.56 crore was mainly on the schemes of ICDS, Rajiv Gandhi National Creche Scheme for the children of working mothers and Swayamsiddha.
2.2       The actual expenditure reported up to 31
st December 2005 is  Rs. 3207.57 crore and by 3rd March, 2006 it reached Rs. 3658.46 crore thereby utilizing 94% of the allocation. The Secretary in her presentation before the Committee informed that the expenditure in 2005-2006 was 100% which means that during the last quarter of the year, remaining balance of Rs.667.72 crore was utilised.
2.3       The Committee would, however, like to point out that in schemes like Rajiv Gandhi National Creche Scheme for the children of Working Mothers, Awareness Generation Programme, Condensed Courses for Women Education, Hostels for Working Women, Short Stay Homes and Nutrition, entire plan allocation in 2005-2006 meant for NER Region has remained unspent.
2.4       Out of the total plan allocation for the Ministry, maximum funds are earmarked for the child welfare schemes whereas the women welfare schemes are getting the benefit of a very small proportion. However, one prominent feature being noticed by the Committee year after year is that there has been optimum utilisation of Plan funds under the child welfare sector in spite of steady increase in the allocation.  In contrast, both allocation and utilisation position in respect of women related schemes shows a declining trend as indicated below:-

2.5       The Committee strongly feels that women welfare related schemes need to be reviewed as a whole to analyse the reasons for this trend of utilisation of funds. Possible reasons can be overlapping of some of these schemes, lack of awareness in the targetted beneficiaries, role of implementing agencies, specially NGOs etc. The Committee would appreciate if such an exercise is initiated by the Ministry at the earliest.
2.6       Status position with regard to Utilisation Certificates (UCs) as given in the Performance Budget (2005-06) of the Ministry highlights a very disturbing trend. The Committee finds that in respect of grants released up to 31
st March, 2004, 5688 UCs amounting to Rs.266.42 crores were pending as on 23rd February 2006. Within a month or so as on 31st March, 2006, number of UCs increased to 6481 involving an amount of Rs.504.27 crore. The earliest period for which the UCs are pending is 1986-87. It seems that position has been simply allowed to aggravate without any initiative taken to control the same so far.
2.7       The Committee would like to be apprised about the pending UCs (State-wise and scheme-wise). The Committee wonders whether any action against the implementing agencies can be initiated now after a lapse of about twenty years or so.            The Committee is of the firm view that financial norms need to be strictly adhered by both the disbursing and implementing authorities. The Ministry should initiate an exercise for procurement of pending UCs without any further delay. The Committee is also of the view that the Ministry should not be satisfied with the timely submission of Utilization Certificates by the implementing
agencies. There is a need for evolving a system of random checking of utilization certificates so as to ensure that funds released are being utilized for the intended purposes. This would also give an idea to the Ministry about the constraints being faced by the implementing agencies in proper utilization of allocated funds.

st January 2006 with different State Governments under ICDS, World Bank assisted ICDS, ICDS Training Programme (Udisha) and Swayamsidha.

of Central funds.
2.10     The Committee would like to have details of expenditure scheme-wise for the year 2005-2006. The Committee also adds that since most of the schemes are run with the assistance of State Governments/NGOs, necessary measures should be taken to coordinate the activities with the concerned implementing agencies so that a transparent picture of detailed expenditure could emerge and a proper feedback helps in understanding the absorption of allocations.
2.11     The Committee would like to draw the attention of the Ministry to the following main strategies to be adopted for various women specific schemes during the Tenth plan to rectify the shortcomings:
Nearly one-fourth of the sanctioned budget allocation of the Department on women specific schemes could not be utilized during the Ninth Plan due to limited capacity of absorption of funds under the existing strategy. This trend must be reversed during the Tenth Plan.
 
All the women’s programmes put together (except the media and publicity) do not cover more than 150 thousand women annually. During the Tenth Plan programmes should be restructured to reach substantially larger number of women.
 
With the introduction of Swarn Jayanti Gramodaya Yojana, Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan and success of National Literacy Mission and National Open School etc., some of the existing schemes like Socio-Economic Programmes, Condensed Courses for Women’s Education and Vocational Training etc have lost their relevance and should be converged with the new institutions/Programmes.
 
There should be two main programmes of the Ministry on women -Women’s Support Services Programmes and Women’s Economic Programmes which should offer a wide range of choices according to the specific situations in different States, regions and sub-regions.
 
2.12     The Committee is constrained to observe that none of the strategies as mentioned above seem to have been implemented upon by the Ministry during the Tenth Plan. Had it been done, some noticeable changes would have been visible by now. Final year of the Tenth Plan has started and position remains unchanged. This is a classic example of how strategies on the paper become fruitless in the absence of strong willpower and mechanism to implement them. The Committee is of the view that these strategies have become all the more relevant in the present scenario. The Committee would appreciate if the Ministry initiates action
without any further delay.
 
III.       INTEGRATED CHILD DEVELOPMENT SERVICES (ICDS) SCHEME
 
3.1       The Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) scheme  provides a package of following services to children below 6 years and pregnant and lactating mothers from disadvantaged sections:
(i)         supplementary nutrition,
(ii)        immunization,
(iii)       health check-up,
(iv)       referral services,
(v)        pre-school non-formal education and
nutrition & health education
 
3.2       It is an ongoing Centrally sponsored scheme implemented through the State Governments with 100 per cent financial assistance from the Central Government for all inputs other than supplementary nutrition which the States were to provide from their own resources. However, the Government of India has decided to provide Central assistance to States for supplementary nutrition also to the extent of 50% of the actual expenditure incurred by States or 50% of cost norms, whichever is less.

However, only 143 APER Projects, reverted to ICDS (General) while the remaining 779 World Bank assisted Projects continued under ICDS III till 31.3.2006. Therefore, funds were reappropriated from ICDS (General) to World Bank assisted Projects ICDS III but within the overall allocation of ICDS and therefore RE was reduced. The BE for 2006-2007 has been kept at Rs. 4454.52 crore  taking into account the existing and anticipated number of beneficiaries for supplementary nutrition.
3.5       The Committee was informed that the Inter-Ministerial Task Force set up in 2004 to review the existing population norms for sanction of an ICDS Project/AWC and suggest revised norms had submitted its reports/recommendations in May 2005. The Committee finds that so far 23 States/UTs have undertaken a micro-level Survey/Planning and forwarded information regarding location specific requirement of additional ICDS Projects and Anganwadi Centres. The Committee has been given to understand that information submitted by some States is incomplete and not in the prescribed format. One year has passed since the
submission of the Report of the Task Force, and the required information is still awaited from States/UTs. The Committee is of the view that the Ministry should make concerted efforts so that AWCs can be set up as per the revised population norms.
3.6       The Committee notes that from 2005-2006, the Government of India were to support States upto 50% of the financial norms or 50% of the expenditure incurred by them on supplementary nutrition. The Committee is surprised to note that the Ministry has not held pre-budget discussions with the States on this issue so far. Ministry’s clarification that States can present their resource position during their discussion on the States Annual Plan with the Planning Commission is not at all convincing.
3.7       In the absence of any detail about the supplementary nutrition met by the States/UTs, it is difficult to assess the impact of the new initiative. The Committee would like to be apprised of the implementation status of this initiative during 2005-06.
3.8       The Committee notes that as on 30.9.05, there are 5365 Operational ICDS Projects and 7,44,887 AWCs indicating a shortfall of 36 ICDS Projects and 22,743 AWCs. During 2005-06, 461 additional Projects and 1,88,055 AWCs were sanctioned. The Committee can understand that setting up of more than 2 lakh sanctioned AWCs will be a long drawn exercise. The Committee also knows that as per the Supreme Court order dated 29th April 2004, there should be an AWC in every human settlement or habitation. The Union of India has to file a notification undertaking the timeframe within which the number of AWCs could be
increased to 14 lakhs, as per the Supreme Court order. The Ministry, however, expressed its inability to notify a period (in years) to cover all 14 lakh AWCs.
3.9       The Committee agrees that increasing the number of Anganwadi Centres from existing 7.44 lakhs to 14 lakhs may be a gigantic task but the Ministry can no longer afford to sit on the problem and delay the process. Instead a plan of action needs to be formulated by the Ministryexpeditiously for achieving the targets set by the Supreme Court. Implementation of the SC directives would catapulate the health of the Indian population comparable to the standards of any of the developed countries. The Committee therefore feels that the Ministry should study the suggestion in its entirety and chalk out a road map to implement the
same. Lack of funds can not be the sole excuse to implement the suggestion. The Committee would also like to be apprised of the reply given to the Supreme Court by the Ministry in this regard. The Committee desires that Anganwadi Centres may be immediately made operational in hemlets and tribal areas where concentration of Dalits, SC/ST population is high.
3.10     Keeping in view the special needs in NE States, the Central Government sanctioned construction of 4800 AWCs at the cost of Rs. 60 crore in 2001-2002 and 7600 AWCs at a cost of Rs. 95 crore in 2002-2003. Another 7600 AWCs at a cost of Rs. 95 crore have been sanctioned in 2004-2005. Further it has been decided to undertake construction of AWCs @ Rs. 1.75 lakh per center. Funds would be allocated out of savings available in the NE component of plan budget of the Ministry. The Committee hopes that in NE States all the AWCs would be provided with  pucca buildings.
3.11     Committee’s attention has been drawn by a nationwide survey of ICDS scheme conducted by theNational Council for Applied Economic Research, covering 60,000 AWCs and 1.8 lakh beneficiary households randomly selected from 36,000 operational ICDS Blocks as on 31.3.96. The study highlighted the following major areas of concern:-
Seven States - Goa (45.1%), Kerala (44%), Karnataka (43.3%), Andhra Pradesh (35.5%), Bihar (34.5%), Maharashtra (33.2%) and Tamil Nadu (25.3%) reported maximum cases of severe malnourished children under 3 years of age.
 
Participation of beneficiary mother is limited to immunization and supplementary nutrition provision (SNP) at Anganwadi centers (AWCs).
 
About 66% and 68% of eligible children and women respectively are registered at AWCs.
 
According to study more than 70% of AWWs, supply of food is irregular at AWCs.
 
On an average about 30% women have received referral service but for children it is less than 10%.
 
Only 40% AWWs are maintaining Community growth charts.
 
About 1/3
rd of AWCs have pucca and semi pucca building.
 
Less than 50% of AWWs are matriculate and above in majority of the Central and Southern States.
 
More than two-thirds of AWWs time is spent on feedings related activities.  Almost no time to spent with the community and for referral services.
 
-           Lack of co-ordination between various departments concerned with child development. Major problem being lack of interest among supervisory growth and low involvement of Panchayats.
 
3.12     The representatives of the Ministry agreed before the Committee that the finding of NCAER about inadequacy of infrastructure are shocking. The children are not very keen to come to Anganwadi Centres because of poor availability of infrastructure. According to them the main reason behind such poor infrastructure is that right from the inception of the scheme in 1975 there was no provision for construction of Anganwadi building; as it was conceived to be a community driven programme.
3.13     The Committee is equally shocked to see the findings of the NCAER. The Committee would like to point out that these findings are not restricted to the infrastructure status of AWCs. It is very clear that each aspect about the AWCs has been assessed and reported upon. This Report has been received by the Ministry sometime in March-April 2005. The Committee hopes that findings of this survey must have been shared with the State Governments and follow-up action started. If not, it may be done at the earliest. The Committee would like to be apprised in this regard at the earliest.
3.14     The Committee notes that as many as 21 responsibilities of Anganwadi Workers recommended by the Core Committee have been circulated to all the States/UTs on 14
th July, 2005.  Besides specific tasks assigned to AWWs, they are also supposed to assist ANMs/PHC staff/ASHA, interact with Panchayat/community.  They are also involved in the implementation of Kishori Shakti Yojana/Nutrition Programme for Adolescent Girls, Pulse Polio Immunization Drive etc.  When asked to specify whether it will be possible for the Ministry to do justice to the duties assigned to AWWs as they are honorary workers from local
community and paid fixed amount of monthly honoraria for rendering services for 4-5 hours a day, the Secretary explained before the Committee that they are also aware of the problems faced by them. The Programme has become very intricate and more and more activities are coming into its ambit because it is an integrated Scheme. But since AWWs are local persons and easily approachable they are exploited by various Departments/Ministries to do the varied jobs.
3.15     The Committee is of the considered opinion that the large number of responsibilities entrusted with the Anganwadi Workers (AWWs) will seriously affect the primary work of the Anganwadi Centres(AWCs) for which they were mainly appointed. With the burden of large number of additional duties the AWW can do justice neither to AWCs nor to the additional responsibilities. The Committee notes that the Central Government provides an honorarium of Rs. 1000 p.m and Rs. 500 p.m to an AWW and AWH respectively. This is quite meager an amount compared to the burden of responsibilities entrusted on them. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the honorarium paid to these two important functionaries of AWCs may be suitably increased. A hike in their remuneration would help in increasing their motivation for better results. Resource constraints should not come in the way of such justified increase.

3.18     The Committee expresses its deep anguish over the large number of vacancies of AWWs, AWHs and Supervisors. It would not be wrong to conclude that the vacancies have hampered the functioning of AWCs and adversely affected the scheme itself. The Committee is not aware about the factors responsible for such a state of affairs. In the absence of these key functionaries, an AWC can not be considered to be operational. This can be accomplished if a strategy is worked out in collaboration with the State Governments/local bodies. Those States which are not willing to follow the time schedule may be pursued on regular basis, if need be, at the highest level, till the vacancies are filled up. The Committee would like to

3.19     The Committee was informed that in addition to emphasis on supplementary nutrition and convergence with health services, special focus is also being given to the pre-school education component of the ICDS scheme, so that the children are fully prepared for entering class I at the age of 6 years under the Sarva Siksha Abhiyan (SSA) & District Primary Education Programme (DPEP). For this, the States have been requested to ensure necessary convergence between ICDS Scheme and SSA & DPEP.
3.20     The Committee is happy to note the decision of convergence between ICDS scheme and SSA & DPEP. The success of ICDS programme depends purely on effective supervision, monitoring, co-ordination and convergence with other Departments and also with better and effective participation of local bodies and community. Convergence of various components is a good idea. The Committee recommends that the revised guidelines, if need be, may be issued without any delay and the State Governments and implementing agencies be pursued for smooth implementation of the converged scheme. Keeping in view the expansion
of the ICDS scheme and its proposed convergence with other programmes, the Committee strongly feels that an effective monitoring mechanism at all levels need to be put in place at the earliest. Only then, services envisaged under ICDS scheme can reach the intended beneficiaries. The Committee would like to be apprised about the steps taken in this direction.
3.21     The Committee notes the observations made in the Mid Term Appraisal of the Tenth  Five Year Plan regarding ICDS, which indicate the absence of the critical component of day-care in the package of services provided. Lack of day-care has its impact on the education of the girl child, since she is made to stay home to take care of younger siblings. The Appraisal also emphasizes that disabled children must be encouraged to attend the crèches and training be given to crèche workers for such children. The Mid Term Appraisal (MTA) further highlights other issues like District level strategies for pre-school education and training
of Anganwadi workers therefor.
3.22     The Committee would like the Ministry to take cognizance of the observations contained in the Mid Term Appraisal and take immediate remedial measures to streamline the scheme. The Committee desires that it may be apprised about the steps taken in this direction.
3.23     The Committee observes that in 17 States/UTs, Co-ordination Committees at state, district, block and village levels have been set up to ensure convergence between ICDS, Health, Drinking Water and Sanitation, Panchayati Raj, Primary Education, Rural Development etc. Welcoming the initiative taken by these 17 States, the Committee would like to point out that NE States, Sikkim, J&K, Orissa and Southern States have not come forward so far. The Committee hopes that with the matter being pursued by the Ministry, these States will be covered very soon.
3.24     The Committee understands that a study on ‘Three Decades of ICDS: An Appraisal’ has been conducted in all the States/UTs. Draft Report was likely to be completed by the end of March 2006. The Committee would like to be apprised about the findings of this study as and when finalised and reported.
 
IV.       TRAINING PROGRAMME UNDER ICDS (UDISHA)
 
4.1       Training is a crucial element in the ICDS scheme. The World Bank assisted ICDS Training Programme, Project UDISHA, was launched from April, 1999. It is a comprehensive training being undertaken through the National Institute of Public Cooperation and Child Development, selected training institutions and the State Governments. The project completed its normal period of 5 years on 30.9.2004 and was extended by the World Bank till 31.3.2006. The Ministry informed that training activities would continue under domestic funds in 2006-2007.
4.2       The plan allocation in BE 2005-2006 was Rs. 40.00 crore and raised to Rs. 82.50 crore due to extension of project from 1.7.2005 to 31.3.2006. The actual expenditure incurred upto 3.3.2006 was Rs. 62.77 crore (Statement VI-BE, RE and Actuals for 2005-06). The Committee would, however, like to point out that on a specific query, the Ministry, while giving the State wise allocation of funds under UDISHA during 2005-06, has informed that as on 16.3.06, there was an expenditure of Rs. 60.99 crores.   The Committee would like to know the acual expenditure incurred under the scheme.
4.3       The Ministry informed the Committee that funds were released to the States on the basis of their physical and financial quarterly progress reports (QPRs) and also keeping in view the trend of utilization and their capacity to utilize the funds by following strict schematic norms for Project Udisha. Therefore there was a slow pace of utilization of funds. Status of allocation of funds to NE States during 2003-04, 2004-05 and 2005-06 reveals that the States failed to take the benefit as these funds have remained underutilized. Not only this, from the details furnished to the Committee it is clear that during 2005-06, financial assistance
was released to NE States only in the last month of the financial year, which is not a healthy sign.
4.4       There is no denying the fact that judicious utilization of the allocation alone would yield desired results. The Ministry can better monitor the utilization by way of getting UCs and monthly progress reports from all the States/UTs and other agencies on quarterly basis. The Committee strongly feels that regular interaction with the States facing constraints will help in achieving the desired results.
4.5       The Committee opines that training is the most crucial element in ICDS as achievement of Programme goals depends upon the effectiveness of frontline workers in improved delivery of packages of services under ICDS. st December, 2005, utilization figures stood  at Rs. 10.03 crores.   However, thereafter, in the last quarter of the year, Rs. 18.47 crore were released.   The Committee is not happy with this uneven spread of fund allocation.   Besides, the Committee  is also constrained  to observe
that allocation meant for NE states has remained underutilized during the last few years, with nil expenditure been reported during 2004-05 and 2005-06. The Committee may be apprised of the reasons for non-utilisation of funds in NE region.

It is expected that every crèche will be inspected at least once in a period of two years.
5.6       The Committee is satisfied with the steps taken to strengthen the monitoring of scheme, but has its reservations about the actual implementation aspect. XVIII.GENDER BUDGETING
18.1     Women face gender specific barriers to access of public services and expenditure. Gender Budgeting lends itself to strengthening of administrative processes and actions achieve the targets for improvement in the position of women. It not only entails a look at allocation of resources for women but goes beyond to cover tracking the utilization of allocated resources, impact analysis and beneficiary incidence analysis of public expenditure and policy from a gender perspective.
18.2     Gender budget has been conceived as one of the tools for achieving the goals and targets set in our plans and policies benefiting women. women.The Committee recommends that the allocation on programmes and schemes benefiting women may be delineated specifically. The Committee also recommends that the components of gender budgeting may be made more clear and included in the guidelines for gender budgeting.

The Committee strongly feels that non-availability of utilization details and availability of unspent balances with the State

The Committee is of the view that in the absence of such a vital information, whatever monitoring  is being done at present cannot be effective enough.   Status of funds released and unspent balances with some State Boards is self-revealing.                                 (Para 6.8)

VII.                 BALIKA SAMRIDDHI YOJANA
 
                        In 2004-05, funds were released to States, however no funds were kept in BE 2005-2006 and 2006-2007. The Ministry has informed that no monitoring/publicity was undertaken at central level.  The Committee observes that total funds released as on 1.3.06 is Rs. 216.15 crore whereas unspent balance as on 30.9.2005 is Rs. 74.97 crore lying with different States like Bihar, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, Orissa and Uttaranchal.      (Para 7.2)
 
                        Earlier the Committee in its 160
th Report had expressed serious concern about the implementation as well as the aspect of uncertainty in the transfer of BSY to the States. The Committee observes that situation instead of improving has worsened since no decision has been taken in this regard so far. The Secretary in her appearance before the Committee also conceded that this was a very unsatisfactory status. (Para 7.3)
 
                        The Committee is not happy with the uncertainty status of the BSY scheme, continuing for so long.  The Committee fails to understand as  why Planning Commission has taken such a long time to take a decision on transferring the Balika Samriddhi Yojana to states.  A decision taken by the Planning Commission at the beginning  of the Tenth Plan is yet to be finalized even though Tenth Plan period is in its  last year. The Committee is also not aware as to how the Committed Liability of Rs. 74.97 crore    lying with different states is going to be adjusted.   The Committee is of the view that this is a classic case of
improper formulation of a scheme launched in haste and inherent flaws being noticed during the course of its implementation.   The Committee does not have much hope about this scheme being effectively implemented by states, with  some States already facing severe financial constraints.   The Committee would once again reiterate that fate of BSY scheme needs to be decided at the earliest.   The Ministry being the nodal authority has to vigorously pursue this issue with the Planning Commission.                                                                                                 (Para 7.4)
 
VIII.    ASSISTANCE FOR CONSTRUCTION/EXPANSION OF HOSTEL BUILDINGS FOR WORKING WOMEN WITH DAY CARE CENTRES FOR CHILDREN
 
The Committee finds that both the financial and physical performance under the scheme have shown declining trend over the years. The utilization has been below the target.   It seems that there is no activity under this scheme in the NE region  as there was an expenditure of only Rs.9 lakhs against an allocation of Rs.1.00 crore in 2004-05 and nil expenditure  has been reported in 2005-06 as on 3.3.2006. The Committee is not aware whether any exercise has been initiated so far to make an assessment about the unsatisfactory performance of this scheme  and take remedial measures.   If not, done so far, the Committee feels that this is
the right time to initiate the same.     (Para 8.1)
 
                        The Committee was informed that there are 40 projects sanctioned from 2001-2002 to 2005-06 in the implementation stage under the Scheme of Working Women Hostel. Out of these projects, in respect of 17 projects, either the file is not traceable or no progress report has been received so far. In majority of these cases, implementing agencies are NGOs.  There are a few  cases where expenditure has already exceeded  the original estimate  and the building project is not yet complete.    The Committee has been informed that in most of the cases, organizations involve their own construction agency for the construction of
hostel building. Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) in its Report No. 2 of 2004 (Para 6.5) has also criticized  the Ministry for its failure to monitor the utilization of grants totalling Rs. 39.58 crores given to NGOs and local bodies for construction of hostels for working women.  The Committee is surprised to note that the requisite information is still awaited from most of the States.                                    (Para 8.2)
 
                        The Committee is of the considered view that the Ministry should not finance such projects or scheme, wherein it has no control over its implementation. In the present scheme, the Committee feels the accountability is lacking and control is missing. Implementation Agencies should not have the sole discretion to select construction agencies.   In any case, projects need to be handled by Government agencies. The Committee would also like to point out that there is an increasing need for setting up more Hostels. If need be, norms for opening of Hostels can be reviewed and revised. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that the scheme needs to revamped and started afresh.                                       (Para 8.4)
 
IX.       SUPPORT TO TRAINING AND EMPLOYMENT PROGRAMME FOR WOMEN (STEP)
 
                        As is evident from above figures, the number of beneficiaries and the number of projects are coming down every year.    The Committee would also like to point out that although overall allocated funds have remained underutilized during the Tenth Plan, performance level has been somewhat different in respect of NE Region States.    Expenditure has been more than the allocated funds for these States.   The Committee would like to have an idea about the status of projects (State-wise) during the Tenth Plan.                                                                                    (Para 9.3)
 
                        The Ministry has cited the inadequate number of staff as one of the reasons for underutilization of funds. Lack of staff for a national level programmes aimed to benefit thousands of women in traditional sectors is hardly a convincing argument. The Committee also notes that the technical team is taking undue time in clearing the projects. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should initiate assessment of the scheme so that procedural bottlenecks can be removed and scheme can be implemented effectively.                                                                            (Para 9.4)
 
X.                    SWAWLAMBAN
 
                        The Committee finds that as many as 1988 utilization certificates are pending with the implementation agencies spread over in different States with the maximum number of UCs being in Andhra Pradesh (321), Uttar Pradesh (206), J & K (180) and M.P. (148).    The Committee is surprised to note that even Central Social Welfare Board has to account for 173 Utilization Certificates.                                     (Para 10.5)
 
                        The Committee in its 160
th Report had expressed its concern that transfer of the schemes not performing well to the States cannot be considered a wise decision.  The Committee is of the view that perhaps no efforts were made by the Ministry to sensitize the State/UTs before the transfer of the scheme.   As per the Performance Budget (2005-06) Rs. 2.00 crore have been provided under the scheme for 2006-07 also. The Committee fails to comprehend the reason for allocating fund for 2006-07 when the scheme stands transferred to the States from 1.4.2006.  The Committee would like the Department to clear the air of
confusion about its committed liabilities as well as the mechanism concerning flow of funds under the scheme.                                             (Para 10.7)
 
XI.       CENTRAL SOCIAL WELFARE BOARD (CSWB)
 
                        The Committee observes that CSWB is entrusted with the implementation of large number of schemes. The assignments have been spread to such an extent that CSWB has failed to devise proper monitoring mechanism for such schemes. CSWB is a central organisation directly under Ministry’s control and it is very surprising to the Committee that the Ministry has not made any effort to strengthen the network of CSWB.   It would be a better situation, according to the Committee, if CSWB is asked to focus its attention on onespecific assignment for a particular period of time. Declining Girl child ratio is a problem which
is assuming alarming proportion nation- wide. The Committee notes some initiative have been taken by a few States for improving the lot of girl child. But some sort of scheme totally dedicated for development of girl child needs to be initiated at national level. The Committee feels that CSWB can play a major role by focusing on this social problem. Nationwide campaign by CSWB in co-ordination with all States Boards and other concerned agencies will have a lasting impact on the thinking of public at large. The issue of huge unspent balances with the different agencies of CSWB would be addressed in case its mandate is
specifically defined. The Committee would, therefore, appreciate if the Ministry identifies some focused subjects for implementation by CSWB.       
(Para 11.4)
 
XII.                 SHORT STAY HOMES (SSHs)
 
                        The Committee observes that a number of Short Stay Homes had to be discontinued due to bad performance.  10 organizations spread over in different States have been issued show cause notices.  This confirms Committee’s apprehension about the shortcomings of a scheme which is meant for the welfare of the down-trodden.   The Committee strongly feels that the Government needs to play a more pro-active role in co-ordination with the State Governments so that the scheme is strengthened. Scheme may therefore be evaluated and revamped.                (Para 12.3)

XIV.                RASHTRIYA MAHILA KOSH (RMK)
 
                        Progress in microfinance activity is pre-dominantly measured in terms of numbers covered, amounts saved, amounts lent and repayment rates, and not by results achieved in genuine economic development. There is need to assess the impact on the upliftment of women. The RMK should evaluate the scheme on these parameters. The Committee recommends that RMK should develop a pool of projects/ schemes/activities which are locally viable and implementable and which can generate income. The RMK can advise the beneficiaries to opt for any of these schemes which will be beneficial for them. The Committee feels
that if such an option is available, the disbursement level will increase and the objectives of the scheme can be achieved.                                  (Para 14.5)
 
                        The Committee was given to understand that a Sub Committee has been setup to examine different aspects of micro credit programmes, economic viability and sustainability of Kosh under RMK.   In this connection, the Committee would like to recall its earlier recommendation with regard to lowering of interest rate on loans to be given by RMK.    The Committee is surprised to note that Governing Body of RMK in its meeting held on 21.12.2005 decided that constitution of a Sub Committee for examination of various operational issues including lowering of interest rate be left to the discretion of MOS, Ministry of
Women and Child Development and  Chairperson, RMK.    The Committee expresses its serious reservation on the handling of such a sensitive issue.    The Committee strongly feels that the existing system under which RMK charges interest@ 8 % on reducing balance from borrowing agency which in turn charges any rate on or above 8% on reducing balance from the ultimate beneficiaries subject to maximum upto 18% needs to be reviewed at the earliest.  One should not forget that the main objective of RMK is to provide micro credit support to poor women.          (Para 14.6)
 
XV.                  NEW  SCHEMES
 
SCHEME FOR RESCUE OF VICTIMS OF TRAFFICKING
 
                        The Committee observes that allocation of Rs. 3.00 crore for this scheme was made in 2004-05 which was reduced to Rs. 30 lakhs in 2005-06.   Allocation in 2006-07 stands at Rs.45 lakhs.  The Committee is not happy with the undue delay in launching of this scheme. The scheme needs more publicity and proper implementation. Since the scheme is to be implemented through NGOs, the Ministry has to be very careful while releasing funds. Monitoring of the scheme is to be strictly followed. The publicity should focus on protection and awareness-raising among parents and guardians.  (Para 15.3)
 
RELIEF AND REHABILITATION OF VICTIMS OF RAPE
 
                        The Committee feels that the victims of rape undergo the conditions of psychological stress and trauma notwithstanding the physical assault. The rehabilitation process of such victim involves psychological support as well as economic assistance. The Committee would like the Ministry to create a separate rehabilitation fund for victims of rape to ensure that they get all sort of psychological and economic assistance in time.                                                                                                   (Para 15.5)
 
XVI.                PREVENTION OF SEXUAL HARASSMENT AT WORKPLACE
 
                        The Government of India constituted a Central Committee under the Chairpersonship of the Secretary, Ministry of Women and Child Development to monitor the implementation of the Supreme Court’s Guidelines for prevention of Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace. The Committee in its Meeting held on 29.10.2002 recommended that Awareness needs to be given on this issue and this task had been assigned to National Commission for Women (NCW) and Central Social Welfare Board alongwith Ministry of Information and Broadcasting. The National Commission for Women has taken up sexual harassment
of women at work place as one of the focal issues in the realm of promotion of gender equality and women's empowerment.  The Commission had widely circulated the Visakha Judgement for compliance along with a code of conduct for workplace formulated by the NCW. The Committee is not aware of the activities/initiatives undertaken by the CSWB and Ministry of Information and Broadcasting to create awareness on the SC Guidelines. This has become all the more important in view of increasing incidents of sexual harassment in BPOs and other private institutions.(Para 16.1)
                                                                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      
                        The Committee is constrained to observe that that the Supreme Court Guidelines had not been properly followed both by the Government Departments.  In a number of cases, Complaint Committees had not been formed.  Where these committees existed, they did not have 50 per cent reservation for women.  Also in many cases the Committees were headed by men instead of women and without the involvement of a third party (NGO).  Lack of awareness among the Members of the complaint Committee was also noticed. The Committee is of the firm view that Supreme Court directive needs to be implemented in letter
and spirit.   The Committee would like to have full details about the 799 organisations covered so far by the NCW alongwith theorganizations where complaint Committees are yet to be set up.    The Committee would also like to have an idea about the additional organizations covered by NCW. The Committee also recommends that the Ministry should come forward with a comprehensive legislation for prevention of sexual harassment in work places. The private institutions may also be brought under the purview of the legislations related to prevention of sexual harassment.   (Para 16.5)
 
XVII.               NUTRITION
 
                        The Committee notes that the FNB provides training to the Anganwadi functionaries. However the Committee notices huge gap between the target and achievement especially in case of training of grassroot level functionaries. The Committee wonders how the Ministry can take a casual approach to the gap reflected and let on increase in the number of malnourished children.                                                                        (Para 17.5)
 
                        The Committee’s attention is drawn by the media reports appearing on regular basis about large number of deaths of children due to malnourishment in the tribal belts of different parts of the country. Such incidents shows the non existence of Government machinery in those areas which can effectively cater to the nutrition requirement of the poor and deprived sections of the Society. The Committee recommends that it is the bounden duty of the Government to ensure that not a single child is dying due to malnourishment especially in view of the facilities being provided through AWCs  under ICDS. The Committee
strongly feels that the FNB needs to train maximum number of functionaries of AWCs so as to sensitize them about the preventive measures to be taken in malnutrition cases of children and mothers. The Committee would appreciate if FNB makes an effective beginning by targetting the functionaries of AWCs located in tribal belts.          (Para 17.6)
 
NATIONAL NUTRITION MISSION (NNM)
 
                        The Committee notes that not much progress has been achieved in the implementation of the scheme. The Committee notes that the objectives of the mission are realistic in nature and if implemented in its totality a healthy child population will be the result. The Committee emphasize that the Ministry should make the scheme functional so as to achieve the desired result of nutrition in a time bound manner.                                      (Para 17.10)
 
XVIII.             GENDER BUDGETING
 
                        The Committee recommends that being the nodal Ministry, the Ministry of WCD should ensure that Gender Budget Cells which are set up in the Ministries have become operational and also pursue this issue with the remaining Ministries.                                                                                                                                             (Para 18.4)
 
The Committee would like to be apprised about the implementation status of the aforesaid initiatives taken by the Ministry.                                      (Para 18.5)
 
                        Committee’s attention has been drawn by the details regarding scheme-wise provisions and physical targets benefiting women in the Budget of Ministry of Women and Child Development as given in the Performance Budget (2006-07). The Committee finds that all the schemes whether targeting children or women have been shown to be providing 100% benefit to women alone. The Committee does not dispute the fact that welfare ofthe child is ultimately the welfare of its mother.However, in view of the emerging concept of child budgeting, it cannot be claimed that flagship schemes like ICDS are benefiting cent
percent women.The Committee recommends that the allocation on programmes and schemes benefiting women may be delineated specifically. The Committee also recommends that the components of gender budgeting may be made more clear and included in the guidelines for gender budgeting.            (Para 18.6)
